title: Catherine Malabou
keyWorks: The Future of Hegel: Plasticity, Temporality and Dialectic (1996)
What Should We Do with Our Brain? (2004)
Ontology of the Accident: An Essay on Destructive Plasticity (2009)
summary: Catherine Malabou (b. 1959) is a French philosopher and a student of Jacques Derrida. Her central concept is “plasticity”: the capacity to receive form (like clay), to give form (like a sculptor) and, in the extreme case, to explode, destroying the previous form (it is no accident that a kind of explosive is called “plastique”). She brings together Hegel, psychoanalysis and neuroscience to understand how a person — their brain, character, personality — changes and yet remains themselves.
onEmotions: For Malabou, feelings are part of how we receive and give form: what we live through leaves a trace in us, but we also shape our own response to it. She distinguishes plasticity from “flexibility”: flexibility means meekly adapting to any demand, while plasticity means changing while keeping the capacity to resist and say “no.” In Ontology of the Accident she also writes about “destructive plasticity”: sometimes a hard event, an illness or a blow of fate changes a person so much that they seem to become someone else — and this new form deserves attention and respect, not only longing for the old one. Her view helps you see yourself not as a fixed character but as a living, ongoing process of formation.

anxiety.text: Catherine Malabou describes the future as what “comes” — and what never comes entirely on schedule. Anxiety wants the opposite: to see the unknown in advance, all of it at once. In The Future of Hegel, Malabou draws on the French expression “voir venir” — “to see what is coming.” It means two things at once: to foresee, and to wait for what will take you by surprise. For Malabou, a real relationship to the future always holds both: some things we can anticipate, but some will arrive unexpectedly — and that is not a failure, it is the very structure of time. Anxiety is an attempt to keep only the first: to foresee everything, to miss nothing. Then you don’t have to see the future in full. Its plasticity lies in the fact that it is shaped by your actions and yet stays open. That openness is frightening, but it is also where there is room to move.
anxiety.practice: Stand at the window for a minute and watch the street: some things you can predict — the bus, someone walking a dog — and some will appear out of nowhere. This is “voir venir”: seeing what is coming and leaving room for surprise.

fear.text: Squeeze a lump of clay in your hand — a dent remains, but the clay doesn’t run. Fear is a natural reaction to what might change or destroy us, and Malabou answers it with exactly this image. Malabou is keen to stress that plastic does not mean formless. The brain, too, changes through experience but keeps its stability. Plasticity is a balance between change and keeping form. Fear often paints things differently: as if one event could leave nothing of you. Through this lens, you have already changed form many times and kept yourself: moves, losses, new roles — somehow you made room for all of it. This is not a promise that nothing frightening will happen. It is a reminder that you have experience of holding your form, even when something presses from outside.
fear.practice: Take something soft in your hand — plasticine, a piece of bread, the corner of a pillow — squeeze it and let go. The mark remains, yet the form holds. Recall one change that you once took in the same way.

sadness.text: Press a seal into warm wax and the pattern stays. Sadness is like such an imprint: something touched you and left a trace, and you don’t need to justify it. Plasticity, for Malabou, begins with its first meaning — the capacity to receive form, like that very wax. What happens to us really does get imprinted: not only in memories, but in the body, in habits, in the way we look at the world. Sadness can be understood as this moment of imprint — when the form is still soft and sensitive to touch. But plasticity has a second meaning too: the capacity to give form. We don’t only receive the trace; we also decide how to hold it. There is no need to rush to “straighten out” your sadness: first let it leave its imprint, and the form you give it will come later.
sadness.practice: Sit quietly for a minute with your palm where the sadness is felt most — as if on warm wax. Don’t straighten it out; just let the imprint be.

grief.text: “Very early in my life it was too late,” writes Marguerite Duras, and Malabou returns to this line when speaking of people changed by loss. Grief is one of the hardest things to live through, and it may be exactly as it is. In Ontology of the Accident, Malabou writes that there are events after which a person changes so much that they no longer recognize themselves. She calls this destructive plasticity — a form born not from growth but from rupture. An important thought for her: this new form is not simply a “damaged version” of the old one but a way of being in its own right, one that deserves attention. If we follow Malabou’s thought, after a loss you don’t have to “get back to your old self.” You can become someone who carries this loss — and that person is you too, no less than before.
grief.practice: Write one sentence that begins with “Since then I…” — without judgment, simply as an observation of your new form.

loneliness.text: A sculptor needs someone to look at the work; so does a form, for Malabou. Loneliness hurts, and it isn’t a matter of weakness. In The New Wounded, Malabou writes about people who have been deeply changed by a traumatic event or illness, and notes how often even those close to them fail to recognize them: the people around them keep addressing the person they used to be and don’t see the new one. Malabou would probably say that loneliness is often the experience of your present form being invisible. You have changed, but the world is still looking at an old photograph. Yet plasticity, for Malabou, is shaped in relationships: the brain and character take form through interaction with others. So loneliness is not a verdict but a sign that your new form needs someone who will see it as it is now.
loneliness.practice: Call or meet someone and tell them not about your past self but about who you have become now — even just one new trait.

anger.text: A sprout breaks through asphalt not because it is aggressive but because it is cramped — Malabou would see plasticity in this. Anger often flares up where something is pressing and deforming you, and it has its own rightness. Plasticity, for Malabou, has a third, explosive meaning — plastique, plastic explosive. Form can not only receive and give but also burst an imposed shell. Malabou insists that this is what distinguishes plasticity from flexibility. A flexible material simply adapts to any pressure; a plastic one is capable of resistance. In other words, anger is not necessarily destruction but a signal that someone is trying to force you into a form that isn’t yours, and something in you refuses. The point is not to explode but to understand which form you want to free yourself from. Then anger becomes not a random blast but a directed force.
anger.practice: Clench your fists and press them against each other for ten seconds — feel a form that resists. Open them and ask: which imposed form do I want to free myself from?

shame.text: Bamboo bends under any wind, while stone keeps its shape; Malabou doesn’t believe a person is obliged to be bamboo. Shame is very heavy, and the wish to hide is easy to understand. In What Should We Do with Our Brain?, Malabou shows how contemporary culture demands endless flexibility: adapt quickly, always be ready for change, have no “rigid” boundaries. Whoever can’t keep up feels like a failure. In effect, part of shame is shame at not being infinitely flexible. But she openly challenges this ideal: a living form has the right to resist, to be slow, to refuse. Your limits are not a defect in the material; they are your very form — what makes you someone rather than just anything.
shame.practice: Name aloud one of your “I can’t” or “I don’t want to” that you feel ashamed of, and add: “This is part of my form.” Listen to how it sounds.

guilt.text: “The wounds of the spirit heal and leave no scars,” wrote Hegel, and Malabou reflects on this line at length. Guilt is a sign that you care how your actions have affected others. Malabou worked extensively on Hegel, for whom spirit is formed through its own actions: we become what we do. An act leaves a trace, and that trace is real. But Hegel also has a famous thought about forgiveness: spirit can work through its deed without freezing in it forever. Malabou reads this as plasticity: a past action gave you form, but did not cast it in bronze. At the same time, she doesn’t ask you to pretend nothing happened — she knows that some wounds leave marks. Guilt can become not a verdict but material from which a new, more attentive form takes shape.
guilt.practice: Do one small thing that gives your guilt a new form: apologize, fix a small thing, make a call. Not everything at once — just one.

quote.text: The wounds of the Spirit heal, and leave no scars behind.
quote.author: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

envy.text: In a museum you see the marble statue but not the workshop — the chips, the failed sketches, the years of work. Envy looks in exactly this way, especially when it seems that everything has worked out for others. Malabou would probably say that envy often compares the incomparable: someone else’s form, seen as ready and finished, with your own, which you know from the inside — with all its doubts and incompleteness. But plasticity means that no form is ever final: behind every visible result there is a person’s own history of receiving and giving form, their own pressures and ruptures. Envy can be turned into a question: what form would I myself like to give to my life? Then it points not to someone else’s life but to your own direction.
envy.practice: Imagine the workshop of the person you envy: what chips, drafts and doubts are lying around? Then ask: what one small step would give my own form something similar?

emptiness.text: In winter a tree looks dead, while under the bark slow work goes on. Emptiness and apathy are a heavy state, when you lack the strength even to want, and Malabou looks at it in a similar way. In The New Wounded and Ontology of the Accident, Malabou carefully describes the experience of a person who, after hard events, becomes seemingly indifferent, cold to what used to move them. She is in no hurry to call this simply a “lack” — for her it is also a form, with its own logic, deserving a respectful look. It follows that emptiness is not your absence but a particular state of your form, perhaps a way of withstanding something that was too much. You don’t need to force yourself to feel right away. Plasticity keeps working in the quiet too: form changes slowly, even when it seems nothing is happening.
emptiness.practice: For a minute, ask nothing of yourself — just notice one very small sensation: the warmth of your palms, the weight of your body, a sound outside.

confusion.text: Inside a cocoon there is no longer a caterpillar but not yet a butterfly, and inside, biologists say, it is almost soup. Confusion resembles this state: the old landmarks have stopped working and the new ones haven’t yet appeared. Malabou opens What Should We Do with Our Brain? by paraphrasing Marx: people make their own history, but they do not know that they are making it. She carries this over to the brain: we are constantly shaping ourselves — through our actions, experience, habits — without realizing it. If we follow Malabou’s thought, confusion can be understood as a moment between forms: the old one no longer holds, the new one is still taking shape. It is uncomfortable, but it is precisely the time of formation. Being lost doesn’t mean you are standing still. Rather, you are inside the work of plasticity, whose result can’t yet be seen.
confusion.practice: Walk a familiar route for five minutes and find one thing you haven’t noticed before. While a form is reorganizing, the way you see changes too.

quote.text: Humans make their own brain, but they do not know that they make it.
quote.author: Catherine Malabou
quote.source: What Should We Do with Our Brain?

fatigue.text: You can bend a paper clip back and forth many times until the metal suddenly snaps — Malabou would say this is how endless flexibility ends. Your tiredness is real and deserves to be taken seriously. In What Should We Do with Our Brain?, Malabou shows that the contemporary economy demands “flexibility” — always being ready to retrain, relocate, restructure, bear any load. Malabou sees a substitution here: flexibility is passive adaptation, while true plasticity also includes the capacity to resist. Burnout can be understood as the limit of flexibility: a material endlessly asked to bend at some point stops responding. It follows that this is not your weakness but a sign that you are not infinitely pliable — and you shouldn’t have to be. Your tiredness is a form that says “enough.”
fatigue.practice: Give your form a rest: lie down for five minutes, rushing nothing and answering no one. If the thought “I should” comes, tell it: “Not now.”

boredom.text: Thousands of steps wear a path through grass, and a year later people walk it without thinking — Hegel called such a groove “second nature.” Boredom can be agonizing when the groove gets too deep: everything is the same, nothing catches hold. Malabou wrote a great deal about Hegel and habit. Habit, for Hegel, is just such a groove: repetition fixes a form and frees up energy, but it can also turn life into a mechanism. In other words, boredom is the feeling of a form that has hardened, when plasticity seems to have frozen. But it hasn’t vanished: the capacity to change remains, even when you can’t see it. Boredom can be heard as a signal: the form that holds you has grown tight. This is not a reason for drastic changes — it is an invitation to a small shift that will remind you that you are still able to take on a new form.
boredom.practice: Step out of the groove by one step today: a different route to the shop, a different cup, a different place to read. Notice how it feels.

joy.text: A child who has just made a lopsided plasticine dog beams — not because it’s perfect but because they made it. Joy is worth living fully, and Malabou helps us see where it comes from. In plasticity, Malabou sees not only the capacity to undergo but also the capacity to give form — as a sculptor gives form to material. In effect, joy is often tied to precisely this second meaning: you feel that you are taking part in how your life takes shape, that you are not only enduring circumstances but also creating something. Even if joy came unexpectedly, it leaves its imprint — for a while the world looks different. You don’t have to analyze it. It is enough to notice: right now you are not only the clay but also the one who shapes it.
joy.practice: Shape something in a minute — out of plasticine, a piece of bread, a napkin. It doesn’t matter what: feel in your hands the joy of giving form.

love.text: Old married couples are said to start looking alike — Malabou would explain this without any mysticism. Love and tenderness change us deeply. In effect, love is plasticity at its clearest: we receive form from another person and give form to them. The people close to us literally sculpt us: our habits, our speech, our way of seeing the world. Malabou stresses that plasticity is not dissolution: a form that receives an imprint keeps itself. In love, this means you can change alongside another without losing yourself, and let them change alongside you. Love is not merging into one but the mutual shaping of two forms, each of which stays alive.
love.practice: Look at the person you love — or recall them — and find one trait that you have probably left in them. Mutual shaping goes both ways.

gratitude.text: An old clay cup sometimes still bears the fingerprints of a potter who lived centuries ago. Gratitude is the moment you notice such prints on yourself: someone has shaped you. For Malabou, a person’s form never takes shape alone: the brain, character, ways of feeling respond to surroundings, to encounters, to care. Her later book Before Tomorrow speaks of epigenesis — development that is not set in advance but unfolds in interaction with the environment. Gratitude can be seen as the moment you notice the hands that took part in shaping you — people, places, chance events. It is not a debt but a joyful recognition: you are the result of many encounters, and that is good.
gratitude.practice: Find one person’s “fingerprint” on yourself — a turn of phrase, a skill, a habit — and send them a short message: “I got this from you, thank you.”

hope.text: A sculptor can’t yet see the whole figure but is already removing the first layer — hope, for Malabou, resembles this work. It is especially needed when the present is hard. In The Future of Hegel, Malabou develops the idea of “voir venir” — the capacity to see what is coming while staying open to the unexpected. The future, for Malabou, is not written in advance, but it isn’t empty either: it is made of what has already begun and of what may arrive. It follows that hope is not certainty about a particular outcome but trust in the plasticity of time and of ourselves. Form can change — Malabou saw this in hard things as well as good ones. Hope rests precisely on this: nothing has hardened for good, and neither have you.
hope.practice: Remove the “first layer” today: one small action toward what you hope for — a call, five minutes of work, a first question.

nostalgia.text: “The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk,” wrote Hegel: wisdom comes when the day has already been lived. Nostalgia — a tender, slightly bitter longing for the past — is a close relative of that owl. Malabou grew out of reading Hegel and knows this thought well: understanding arrives when a form of life has already grown old. We only really begin to see what a period of our life was once it has passed. If we follow Malabou’s thought, nostalgia is this kind of evening gaze. Earlier forms have not vanished without a trace: plasticity means precisely that what we have lived through stays in us as an imprint, onto which new layers settle. The past is not a lost copy but a part of your present form.
nostalgia.practice: Read Hegel’s line about the owl of Minerva aloud and recall one detail from the past that you miss. Ask: what of it lives in me now?

quote.text: The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk.
quote.author: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

craving.text: Neuroscientists say that neurons that fire together wire together — Malabou reads this phrase as a philosophical discovery. A craving — a sharp “I want it right now” — can be very strong, and it is not your fault that it comes. Malabou, following Hegel, thought a great deal about habit. Habit is “second nature”: repetition wears a groove in us, and the body starts moving along it by itself. Then a craving is not a whim or a weakness of character but the force of an established form. But form, for Malabou, is plastic: what was shaped by repetition can gradually be reshaped. A craving doesn’t stay still, either — it rises, peaks and falls away, like a wave. You might try neither fighting it nor giving in right away, but watching: what is this wave carrying, and what are you really missing?
craving.practice: When a craving comes, set a timer for five minutes and watch the wave like weather: rising, peaking, falling. Every wave you let pass reshapes the groove a little.

addiction.text: A rut in the road helps the wheel roll — and keeps it from turning; Malabou, following Hegel, sees both of these forces in habit. Addiction is not a moral failure. It is a long-standing loop, and getting out of it is hard, not for lack of willpower. Reading Hegel, Malabou shows the double nature of habit: it can free us — we don’t have to think through every movement anew — and it can also bind us, when a form hardens and begins to lead us on its own. In other words, addiction is a form that has become fixed and organized a life around itself. But plasticity means that what has been fixed can gradually be reshaped. It is a long process, and Malabou stresses that form takes shape in relationships — not alone. Your character is not sentenced to its present form, even if right now that form seems very solid.
addiction.practice: Tell one person you trust what role this habit plays in your life — what it gives you or replaces. If you need wider support, find out about the nearest mutual-help group: form changes in relationships.

hangover.text: “Was that really me?” — Malabou explores this question seriously, though she writes about changes far more dramatic than one evening. The morning after can be very hard: feeling unwell, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. None of this is a reason to punish yourself. Malabou writes about an unsettling experience: not recognizing yourself, meeting someone unfamiliar within you. The hungover “what did I do last night?” is a small echo of that experience. In effect, one evening doesn’t define your form. A person’s form takes shape over a long time and out of many layers; one event leaves a trace but doesn’t rewrite you entirely. There is no need to pass judgment on yourself now. It is enough to gently find your footing again: you are here, you are the same person, and you have today.
hangover.practice: Come back into today’s form through your body: a glass of water, an open window, your hands under warm water. Name three facts aloud: where you are, what time it is, what you’ll do in the next hour.

euphoria.text: A kernel of corn in a hot pan suddenly bursts and becomes twice its size. A burst of euphoria is similar: everything seems possible, and there’s no need to spoil it. In effect, euphoria is an experience of the explosive side of plasticity: as if the old frames had burst and your form had opened wider than usual. This really does say that you are capable of more than you are used to thinking. Malabou reminds us of something else too: plasticity is not only explosion but also the capacity to hold form. Euphoria is short by nature, and knowing this doesn’t mean devaluing it. On the contrary: you can live this moment more fully if you don’t demand that it last forever, and keep from it whatever you’d like to take with you.
euphoria.practice: Write down one thought that came to you on this high — so that later, in your everyday form, you can return to it calmly.

crash.text: After a concert, sound still hangs in the empty hall — musicians call it the after-ring. A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid event — is very unpleasant, and it happens to almost everyone. In Malabou’s terms, the plastic form that opened up during the high is returning to a more stable state. The distinction matters to Malabou: an elastic material returns to exactly its former shape, while a plastic one keeps something of what it went through. So the comedown is not a return “to zero.” You haven’t simply fallen back; something of the high has stayed in you, even if you can’t feel it right now. The drop is a time when form settles and reorganizes. You don’t need to force yourself to take off again. You can give yourself time to settle.
crash.practice: Let your form settle: sit for five minutes in silence with nothing switched on, and look inside for the “after-ring” of the high — one small thing that has stayed.

panic.text: A bridge sways in a strong wind but holds: that is what it was built for. Panic is like such a wind — your heart pounds, your breathing falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. It follows that in panic you feel the threat of your form exploding: as if you are about to stop holding together. But Malabou stresses that plasticity is not only the capacity to change but also the capacity to keep form under pressure. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it passes, you can lean on what is holding your form right now: your body, the floor under your feet, your out-breath. You don’t have to understand what is happening — it is enough to wait out the wave.
panic.practice: Press your palms together and push — feel your hands holding their form. Put your feet on the floor, take a few out-breaths longer than the in-breaths, and name aloud three objects you can see.

dread.text: Michelangelo’s “Slaves” remain half inside the marble: not yet out, but no longer stone. Existential dread — “what is all this for,” the sense of an abyss — is one of the hardest feelings, and Malabou doesn’t avoid it. In Ontology of the Accident she writes that life is vulnerable to the accidental, that any event can change us unpredictably. But her view doesn’t lead to despair. It follows that if form is not guaranteed, it is not predetermined either. The same plasticity that makes us vulnerable lets us give form, create, change. The abyss you feel is the other side of openness: the world is not finished, and neither are you. There is no answer to “what for” here, but there is room for an answer to take shape.
dread.practice: Give form to one small thing right now: fold a paper bird, move a flowerpot, make the bed. The world isn’t finished — and now this small thing is in it.

fomo.text: A sculptor who is afraid to chip away even a sliver of marble will be left with a block. The fear of missing out keeps us in front of such a block: it feels as though life is happening somewhere you are not. In What Should We Do with Our Brain?, Malabou criticizes the culture of “flexibility,” in which a good person is someone always connected, always ready for a new opportunity, able to be everywhere at once. It follows that the fear of missing out is an internalized demand for endless flexibility. But true plasticity involves choosing a form: for something to become yours, you have to not choose a great deal. A form that tries to take in every possibility stops being a form. Missing out is not a failure but the condition for having a life of your own at all.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you are consciously giving up today — an event, a feed, a chat — and say aloud: “I’m chipping this away.” Then turn to what remains.

sleepless.text: A potter’s wheel spun during the day keeps turning at night after the potter has gone. Thoughts at three in the morning are like that: insomnia is agonizing, and everything feels heavier than in the daytime. In other words, night thoughts are a form that keeps spinning on its own, along a familiar groove, once the outer support of the day is gone. Malabou reminds us that the brain is not a machine running a single program but a plastic form, responsive to what happens to it. At night it helps not to argue with your thoughts but to give them an outer form — to move them out of your head onto paper, where they become finite. This doesn’t solve every problem; it is a gentle way of telling your thoughts: I’ve written you down, you can wait until morning.
sleepless.practice: Keep a notebook nearby and jot the spinning thoughts down in short words, one line each. Close the notebook: the wheel has stopped until morning.

betrayal.text: In Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Daphne turns into a laurel and can never be what she was — Malabou thinks often about such transformations with no way back. Betrayal wounds just as deeply: it destroys not only a relationship but also trust in the world. In Ontology of the Accident, Malabou writes about events that don’t merely upset us but break our former form — after them, a person becomes someone else. In effect, betrayal is such a rupture: the former “you,” who trusted in just that way, won’t come back. That is painful to admit. But Malabou sees more than loss in the new form. You don’t have to restore your former innocence, but you don’t have to freeze in suspicion either. You can find a form of trust that remembers the experience of betrayal and still stays alive.
betrayal.practice: Tell someone you trust one thing this event has taught you about your own boundaries — without reproaching yourself. What is said aloud takes on form.

jealousy.text: A sculpture can be cast in bronze and will never change again — but you can’t do that with a living person, Malabou reminds us. Jealousy is agonizing: fear and love are mixed in it. In effect, jealousy is partly born of the wish for another person’s form to be fixed, unchanging and ours. But people are plastic: they change through encounters, experience, time. This plasticity can’t be forbidden — you can only take part in it. Malabou insists that plasticity is bound up with freedom: the capacity to resist someone else’s form is part of being alive. Jealousy can be understood as fear of another person’s freedom. And then the question is not “how do I hold on” but “how do I stay close to someone who is changing” — while allowing yourself to change too.
jealousy.practice: When you feel ready, ask your partner: “How are you changing these days? What’s new in you?” — and listen without checking. This is how you take part in someone else’s plasticity.

resentment.text: A tree that once had a nail driven into it slowly grows bark around it — the wound becomes part of the trunk. An old resentment is similar: you carry it with you, and it speaks the truth about something important. Through this lens, resentment is a form cast around a wound. It preserves the memory of pain and protects against it happening again. Malabou, who wrote extensively about traumatic events in The New Wounded, doesn’t pretend that every wound heals without a trace; some become part of one’s form. But plasticity means that even a hardened form can be reshaped — not cancelled, not forgotten, but remolded. You can keep the knowledge of what happened to you and still free yourself from having to carry it as a constant weight.
resentment.practice: Find where in your body the resentment lives, rest your palm there and breathe out slowly. Ask: what is it protecting me from — and could I get that protection some other way?

heartbreak.text: Hold a lump of clay in your hand long enough and it takes the shape of your palm, keeping it even after your fingers open. A broken heart really hurts, and Malabou explains why. A breakup is not only the loss of a person but also the loss of a form you created together: shared habits, private words, plans. It follows that two people give each other form, and after a breakup you carry its imprint. This explains why it hurts so much: a part of you is being broken. But plasticity also means that the imprint doesn’t make you incomplete. It becomes part of your story, and a new form begins to take shape — slowly, sometimes imperceptibly. There is no need to rush to “forget.” You can let yourself be a person whom this relationship has changed.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one thing you carried away from this relationship — a habit, a turn of phrase, a recipe — and do it today as something of your own.

impostor.text: Every master once sat over their first lopsided pot — Malabou insists that among people there are no finished products. The feeling that you are about to be found out comes when you forget this. Malabou writes about a culture that demands we be endlessly flexible, ready for any role, always competent. If we follow Malabou’s thought, impostor syndrome arises when you feel yourself to be in the process of formation while the demands say you should already be a finished product. But plasticity means that no one is a finished form. Everyone you consider “the real thing” is still being formed too. Your sense of incompleteness is not proof of fraud but an honest feeling that you are a living person who is learning, not a cast statue. In essence, there is nothing to expose: incompleteness is everyone’s shared condition.
impostor.practice: Ask someone you consider a “real” professional what they once couldn’t get right. Listen to the story of their workshop.

self_hatred.text: The critic looks at you as a cracked statue to be thrown out — while Malabou sees a person as clay that is still being worked. A cruel inner voice is exhausting, and you deserve gentleness — including your own. In other words, the inner critic thinks of you as a frozen form with an incurable defect: “this is what you are, and this is what you’ll always be.” But Malabou’s whole philosophy contradicts this. A person is not a finished statue but a process of formation, holding traces of the past, the pressure of circumstances and your own capacity to give form. The critic’s verdict is an attempt to stop plasticity. Its voice does not tell the truth about you; it speaks of pain that has hardened. You are more than this frozen judgment.
self_hatred.practice: Say aloud one sentence from your inner critic, and then the answer: “This is not a final form. I am still changing.” Repeat the answer three times, slowly.

helplessness.text: A blade of grass in a crack in concrete can’t move the slab, but it can grow toward the light. Feeling powerless to change anything is very hard, and it often reflects real circumstances. Malabou doesn’t deny that the accidental exists: in Ontology of the Accident she writes about events that arrive unasked and that we did not choose. She doesn’t demand omnipotence of anyone. But plasticity, for Malabou, never disappears completely, even in the tightest circumstances: at least a tiny capacity to give form remains — to your attitude, to a small action, to your choice of words. In other words, being powerless to change everything is not the same as being powerless to change anything. You can lean on the very smallest thing.
helplessness.practice: Give form to the smallest thing within your power: straighten your back, take a sip of water, say one kind word to yourself. Notice: you did this yourself.

procrastination.text: A shapeless lump of clay is more daunting than a finished sketch: it’s unclear which side to approach it from. “I can’t get started” is a painful state, and it doesn’t mean you’re lazy. In effect, procrastination is sometimes a quiet resistance to an imposed form. Malabou distinguishes flexibility — meek adaptation — from plasticity, which includes the capacity to refuse. If a task feels alien, oppressive, shapeless, just this kind of resistance may wake up in you. There is another possibility: the task has no form yet, and it is too hard to get hold of. Then it isn’t a matter of willpower but of giving the task a small, concrete form. Procrastination is worth not scolding but hearing: what in me is resisting — and resisting what? The answer often suggests where to begin.
procrastination.practice: Pinch off a five-minute piece of the task — one paragraph, one call, one page — and do only that. The form will appear as you work.

uprooted.text: Catherine Malabou was born in Algeria and has lived her life in France — the question of how to remain yourself in a new place is not abstract for her. Being cut off from home is a profound experience: along with the place go language, habits, a sense of solid ground. Then moving is one of the strongest tests of plasticity: you take on a new form — a new language, new rules — while trying to keep the old one. Malabou insists that plasticity is not dissolution but holding on to form through change. You don’t have to either assimilate completely or freeze in the past. You can become a person in whom both places live — and this new form is not worse than the old, just different.
uprooted.practice: Cook or buy something from your old home today and eat it slowly in your new place. Two forms can live in one person.

overload.text: Wax stamped with seal after seal eventually stops holding any of them. Overload is real: the endless feed, notifications and information noise are draining. In What Should We Do with Our Brain?, Malabou, drawing on the sociologists Boltanski and Chiapello, describes a world of networks in which a good worker is one who is always connected and ready to switch. She sees this as a demand for flexibility passed off as freedom. Her answer is plasticity, which also includes the capacity to disconnect, to say “no.” Through this lens, your overload is not an inability to cope but a sign that a form cannot take on infinitely many imprints. Choosing what to let pass is a way of keeping your form.
overload.practice: Turn your phone face down and for five minutes let the wax cool: no new imprints, just quiet. Notice how the feeling in your head changes.

unreality.text: Spinoza told of a Spanish poet who, after an illness, could not believe that the plays he had written were his own; Malabou sees in this story a key to the psyche’s strange transformations. The feeling that nothing around you is quite real is frightening and disorienting too, and it deserves to be described gently. In Ontology of the Accident, Malabou offers an interesting thought: sometimes, when a real way out of a hard situation is impossible, the psyche finds its own form of escape — it detaches, as if stepping back from what is happening. It follows that the sense of unreality can be such a form of protection rather than a sign that you are disappearing. There is no need to fight the feeling by force. You can gently restore your connection with the world through simple things: touch, sound, the weight of your body. A form that has stepped back can just as gradually return.
unreality.practice: Slowly name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear. Form comes back through the senses.

awe.text: A glacier carves a valley over centuries, and a person stands before it for a minute — and something in them changes shape too. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious state. In Self and Emotional Life, written with Adrian Johnston, Malabou turns to Descartes, for whom the first of the passions was wonder — the capacity to be struck by something new, before we have decided whether it is good or bad. If we follow Malabou’s thought, awe is plasticity in its purest form: you are open to receiving form from something larger than you. Such an experience doesn’t need to be explained or put to use. You can simply let it leave its trace — for it really does change, even if only a little, the way you see the world.
awe.practice: Stand for a minute before what filled you with awe, doing nothing and taking no photos — let it leave its imprint.

relief.text: Steel that has carried a load is never quite the same afterwards — engineers call it residual deformation. Relief is when something that was pressing on you finally lets go, and it is worth living fully. Malabou would probably say that relief is the moment when the pressure on your form eases. Malabou distinguishes elasticity from plasticity: an elastic material returns to exactly its former shape after a load, while a plastic one keeps something of what it went through. So relief is not simply a return to how things were before the anxiety. You have come out of the tension a little different: perhaps having learned that you are able to endure. You can let yourself relax and also notice what has changed. Relief is not only the end of something hard but also a quiet sign of your own resilience, worth acknowledging.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath, open your shoulders and ask: what do I know about myself now that I didn’t know before this strain?

calm.text: A potter leaves a finished pot on the shelf so the clay can dry in peace — without this pause the form won’t hold. Calm is such a pause, and it is worth protecting. In other words, calm is the moment when a form holds itself: it isn’t being pushed from all sides, it doesn’t have to bend or resist. Malabou stresses that plasticity is not endless change but a balance of change and stability. Calm is the feeling of a stability in which form rests. Such moments matter no less than moments of growth: it is in them that experience settles and earlier imprints find their place. Calm doesn’t need to be earned or immediately put to use. You can simply be in your form for a while, without asking what to do with it next.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, sensing the outline of your body — where it touches its support, where it ends. Change nothing; let the form dry.

inspiration.text: Michelangelo is credited with saying: “I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free.” Inspiration is like that moment: you want to create, and you want it to last. For Malabou, plasticity is also the capacity to give form, as a sculptor does, and the word itself recalls the plastic arts. In effect, inspiration is a moment when you feel especially keenly that you are the one who shapes, not only the one being shaped. But she also reminds us that form is born of an encounter: artist and material act on each other. Inspiration doesn’t come out of nowhere — it responds to what you have lived through. You can trust it and give it material to work with.
inspiration.practice: In five minutes, sketch one form that inspiration suggests — a drawing, a plan, a melody — without polishing it.

schadenfreude.text: When the house next door floods, it’s hard not to breathe out: “not mine.” Schadenfreude — the secret pleasure in someone else’s failure — is familiar to almost everyone, and people are usually ashamed of it. But the feeling itself says little about who you are. In Ontology of the Accident, Malabou insists that any of us can at any moment be struck by an accident — an illness, a loss, a blow — that changes us beyond recognition. We are all equally fragile, even though we try not to notice it. Then schadenfreude partly protects us from this thought: “it happened to them, not to me.” And in the culture of endless flexibility and comparison that she criticizes, someone else’s fall also briefly eases the pressure on you. If you see in schadenfreude a fear for your own form, it becomes more understandable — and gentler.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, breathe out and silently wish that person — and yourself — the strength to stand. We are all equally fragile.

contempt.text: A death mask fixes a single expression forever — a living face can’t do that. Contempt, a cold look from above, turns the other person into such a mask; it often protects against disappointment, powerlessness, pain. Malabou’s central thought is that people are plastic: they take on form, change, can become different. Through this lens, contempt does the opposite — it casts the other person in a frozen form: “that’s what they are, and they’ll never be anything else.” In The New Wounded, Malabou notes how often people fail to see someone else’s change and keep addressing the old image. Contempt is a similar blindness, only a chosen one. At the same time, it can also protect your own form — what you don’t want to become. You don’t need to force yourself to respect someone you despise. But you can notice that you are freezing along with them.
contempt.practice: Imagine this person ten years from now: who might they become? One thought about their capacity to change — and the mask thaws a little.

disgust.text: A cell lives as long as its membrane decides what to let in and what not; Malabou reminds us that a living form has the right to say “no.” Disgust is a very bodily feeling: toward a situation, toward people, sometimes toward yourself. The body recoils before thought does, and there is nothing shameful in that. Plasticity, for Malabou, is not endless pliability. Form receives imprints, but it also knows how to refuse: not everything can or should be let in. Malabou insists that the capacity to resist is what distinguishes living plasticity from submissive flexibility. It follows that disgust is one of form’s most ancient ways of saying “no”: it is a boundary that form guards. If disgust is directed at yourself, it often means that you don’t recognize some new form of yours — after an illness, a hard period, a change. That form is not worse than the old one; it just needs time to become your own.
disgust.practice: Step back from whatever your body is recoiling from and tell yourself: “This is where my boundary runs.” Don’t judge it — just note it.

revenge.text: A wounded tree can grow new bark or send out a shoot in another direction — it doesn’t need to answer a blow with a blow. The wish for revenge makes sense: you have been hurt, and you want the person who hurt you to feel the same. Malabou would probably describe revenge as the wish to return the imprint: they left a mark on me — let the same mark be left on them. But plasticity, Malabou reminds us, is not only the capacity to receive form but also the capacity to give it. Revenge quietly continues the old dependence: your response is still being shaped by the one who wounded you. A plastic response is a question: what form do I myself want to give to what happened to me? You can acknowledge the wish for revenge itself without handing yourself over to it.
revenge.practice: Imagine yourself as the sculptor of your response: what form do you want to give to what happened — a boundary, protection, a demand for justice? Choose one and take a small step toward it.

anger_at_loved.text: Two people who have been shaping each other for years inevitably bump elbows. Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can be sharp, and then shame arrives, though it doesn’t cancel love. Malabou would probably say that those close to us are the ones who shape us most, and we shape them. Such mutual shaping never happens without friction. Malabou, following Hegel, writes of habit as “second nature”: in families and couples, grooves form — roles, tones of voice, old scripts — and we fall into them despite ourselves. Anger sometimes flares when the form you have become runs up against an old groove: “I’m not that child anymore,” “I don’t want to be just a function.” This is no reason to hurt the people you love, but it is a reason to hear which role you are tired of.
anger_at_loved.practice: Once you’ve cooled down, say to them not “you always…” but “I’m tired of being…” — and name a role, not a person.

ambivalence.text: A potter presses the clay and at the same time supports it from the other side — otherwise the wall collapses. Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a similar double effort, tangled and heavy, and you want to finally understand which is true. Malabou grew out of reading Hegel, for whom contradiction is not an error of thought but the engine of life. One of Hegel’s key words is sublation (Aufhebung), which means both “to cancel” and “to preserve.” Malabou shows that plasticity works the same way: a form holds opposites together — receiving and giving, changing and remaining itself. In other words, mixed feelings toward someone close are a living form of connection, not a malfunction. Attraction and resistance are both at work in it, and both forces are doing something for you. They don’t have to be reconciled right away. Sometimes what matters is simply letting them coexist.
ambivalence.practice: Hold your hands as if shaping a pot on a wheel: one presses from outside, the other supports from within. Stay like this for a minute — attraction and resistance can work together.

guilty_relief.text: A hand that has long gripped a heavy load doesn’t open right away — and then the fingers straighten by themselves. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes with shame, but relief and love can live side by side. In effect, a long, hard situation — caring for someone who is ill, an exhausting relationship — gives a person a form: they become someone who is always holding on, enduring, waiting. That pressure was real. When it disappears, the form begins to straighten out, and relief is the natural response of a material from which a load has been lifted. It is not a betrayal but a sign of how hard it was. Malabou also reminds us of traces: what we have lived through doesn’t vanish without a trace. Your love and your care remain in you, even now that it has become easier to breathe.
guilty_relief.practice: Slowly clench and open your fists a few times and tell yourself: “I feel lighter — and that doesn’t cancel what I loved.”

indifference.text: A frozen river isn’t dead: water flows under the ice, you just can’t hear it. Sometimes something happens that “should” move you — and inside it is quiet, and on top of the indifference comes worry: “Am I heartless?” In The New Wounded, Malabou argues against psychoanalysis’s habit of looking for a hidden meaning behind every state. She writes that sometimes coldness and indifference are neither a secret repressed desire nor a moral flaw, but simply the trace of what one has been through: a form changed by an event or by overload. Then your indifference doesn’t have to “expose” anything about you. There is no need to squeeze out the feelings you’re supposed to have. It is enough to notice this quiet without judgment and give it time — a living form begins to respond again in time.
indifference.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes, as if by a frozen river, squeezing nothing out of yourself. Say: “I don’t feel it right now — and that isn’t forever.”

escape.text: A spring held compressed for a long time leaps out of your hand at the first chance. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and leave can be just as strong. It is legitimate: this is often how a form speaks when it has been squeezed for too long. Malabou distinguishes flexibility from plasticity. Flexibility means adapting to any demand for as long as your strength lasts. Plasticity is the capacity to change while keeping the right to say “no” and to give yourself a new form. Through this lens, the wish to run away is often born where you have long been asked for nothing but flexibility: you bent, and now it seems the only way out is to leave altogether. But plasticity offers other moves too: changing a role, a boundary, a rhythm. Malabou doesn’t decide for you whether to leave or stay. She helps you understand what form you want to take.
escape.practice: Imagine you have already left: what exactly were you finally able to do? Name it in one word — it’s a hint about the form you are missing here.

forbidden_attraction.text: The smell of lilac in spring stops you in the street against your will — the body responds before the mind. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” also comes unasked and often brings turmoil, as if the feeling itself were already a transgression. But attraction doesn’t ask permission, and it says little about your integrity. In Before Tomorrow, Malabou examines the notion of epigenesis: the form of a living being is not entirely laid down in advance but takes shape through encounters with its environment. It follows that attraction is one such encounter: another person leaves an imprint on you before you have had time to decide whether you want it. This is the first side of plasticity — receiving form. But there is also the second — giving form: you yourself decide what to do with this imprint and how to understand it. Attraction can be explored with curiosity: what exactly in me is responding?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what part of me does this person awaken — courage, lightness, tenderness? Think about how you could give that part a form in your own life, without them.

social_anxiety.text: Every calm encounter, even one that lasts half a minute, leaves its trace in the brain — Malabou builds a whole philosophy on this fact of neuroscience. Fear of people and their judgment — the stiffness, the wish to become invisible — is exhausting, and you are not alone in it. In What Should We Do with Our Brain?, Malabou describes a world where a person must constantly “present themselves”: stay connected, make an impression, make contacts easily. If we follow Malabou’s thought, social anxiety is partly a response to this demand to be endlessly flexible and pleasing to everyone. Your form has the right to be awkward, slow, quiet. Malabou reminds us of something else too: plasticity means that experience leaves traces. Fear is not a final form but a groove, and beside it you can gradually wear a different path.
social_anxiety.practice: Arrange one tiny calm encounter today: ask a shop assistant something or nod to a neighbour. It’s one more step on a new path.

uncertainty.text: In the seventeenth century scientists seriously looked for a tiny ready-made person inside the embryo — Malabou recalls this debate for a reason. Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen — is hard: the mind tries to calculate everything in advance. In Before Tomorrow, Malabou contrasts two old ideas about how living things develop. Preformationism held that the whole future is already contained, ready-made, in the embryo. Epigenesis held that form takes shape gradually, through interaction, and is not predetermined. Malabou sides with epigenesis. Malabou would probably say that uncertainty is not a malfunction but the normal state of a living form: the future isn’t written because it is still being created — by you among others. That is unsettling, but it is also freedom. You don’t need to know in advance who you will become in order to take the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Say aloud: “This isn’t decided yet, which means…” — and finish the sentence with a possibility, not a threat.

waiting.text: Plaster in a mould takes about twenty minutes to set, and no impatience will speed it up by a second. Waiting — for an answer, results, news — is also a time of setting: it is wearing, time stretches out, and it is hard to live an ordinary life. Malabou’s first book is called The Future of Hegel: Plasticity, Temporality and Dialectic: for her, plasticity is inseparable from time. A form needs time to take shape, as clay needs time to set, and experience needs time to become part of character. In other words, waiting is not an empty gap between events but also a time of formation: you are already changing as you prepare to meet different outcomes. Malabou speaks of “voir venir” — the ability to see what is coming while also waiting for what may surprise you. While waiting, you can stop hurrying the outcome and notice who you are becoming as you wait.
waiting.practice: Give your hands a slow task that also needs time to set: knead some dough, water the seedlings, brew tea and wait until it has steeped.

regret.text: An old vase can be glued back together, or its shards can become a mosaic — a different thing, made of the same material. Regret over what you did or didn’t do can keep coming back for years — “if only I had acted differently back then…” — and it shows what mattered to you. Reading Hegel, Malabou stresses that the past doesn’t disappear: it stays in us as form, as habit, as trace. For Hegel, the past is “sublated” — preserved and at the same time transformed in the present. In effect, regret is not only pain over what is impossible but also material: you can’t change that act, but you can give form to what it means to you. A regret that lives on is a sign that you are no longer the person who made that mistake. Your present form is able to understand more.
regret.practice: Write down one regret and beneath it: “Today I understand…” — one sentence about what you have learned since.

longing.text: A ring worn for a long time leaves a pale band on the finger — visible even after the ring is taken off. Longing for a particular person is like that band: you miss their voice, their familiar gestures, their presence beside you. Then someone close to you has left an imprint on you — not a metaphorical one but a very real one: in your habits, your words, the way you look at the world. Malabou stresses that plasticity is the capacity to keep a form once received. Longing is the feeling of this imprint when the person is not there: your form feels its own outline where there used to be a touch. It hurts, but it is also evidence that the encounter really changed you. You don’t have to chase the longing away; you can gently acknowledge: this person is part of my form.
longing.practice: Do one thing today “their way”: make tea the way they did, use their turn of phrase, walk their favourite route. The imprint lives on in action.

world_pain.text: Sea water leaves salt even on the rocks the waves reach only in a storm. Pain for the world — hard news, wars, injustice — settles in us in a similar way and can overwhelm you so much that it’s hard to live your own life. In The New Wounded, Malabou writes about people changed by traumatic events and notes that the line between personal and collective wounds is blurred: catastrophes, violence, exile leave traces not only in history but in the psyches of individual people. Through this lens, your pain is a sign that you are open to the world, that its events leave an imprint on you too. But plasticity is not only receiving form but also holding it. You can respond to the world’s pain without letting it destroy you. For that you need pauses, support, and people to share it with.
world_pain.practice: Put the news aside for an hour and give a few minutes to what supports your form: a conversation, a walk, work with your hands.

rejection.text: Clay set aside by one potter can become another’s finest bowl. Rejection hurts: it feels as though you have been told “you don’t fit,” and it wounds you to the core. Malabou wrote a great deal about Hegel, and for Hegel a person becomes themselves through recognition by another: self-consciousness needs another self-consciousness. That is why being denied recognition hurts so much — it isn’t a whim. But for Hegel recognition is not one decision by one person; it is a long, mutual process involving many. It follows that one “no” is an imprint but not your whole form. You remain plastic: you are also shaped by other encounters, those in which you are seen and accepted. You can live through rejection as a wound without turning it into a final verdict on yourself.
rejection.practice: Call someone who accepts you as you are — or at least spend a minute with them in your thoughts.

abandonment.text: Fired clay holds its shape without the potter’s hands — that is what the firing was for. The fear of being abandoned can be tenacious: any pause in contact seems like the beginning of the end, and behind it is a real need for a secure connection. If we follow Malabou’s thought, this fear often pictures you as a material with no form of its own: as if without the other you would crumble, like unset clay without support. But Malabou insists: plastic does not mean formless. A plastic form receives the imprints of others and yet keeps itself — holds its own shape. The people close to us really do shape us, and their leaving hurts. But the form you have become is yours; it won’t vanish along with someone’s presence. This thought doesn’t cancel the fear, but it can give it something to lean on.
abandonment.practice: Rest your hands on your knees, feel your weight and tell yourself: “My form holds me.”

unrequited.text: Galatea came alive for Pygmalion — in life, marble more often stays silent. Unrequited love hurts in a special way: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. And often the question arises beside it: “What is wrong with me?” Malabou would probably say that love is always an event of plasticity: we receive form from the one we love, even if they don’t know it. Being unrequited doesn’t make this process any less real: you really did change, open up, discover something new in yourself. And the second side of plasticity is the capacity to give form. A love that received no answer can become something you create: a letter you don’t have to send, a song, an act, a new understanding of yourself. You can grieve what didn’t come true and at the same time respect the form this love has given you.
unrequited.practice: Give this love a form that needs no answer: sketch a drawing, play a tune, do a kindness for someone else. Love can become something you create.

humiliation.text: Try to cram a living plant into a pot that is too small and it will push back — that stubbornness speaks of life. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it is as if you were forcibly pressed into someone else’s form, smaller than you are. The blame for this does not lie with you. Malabou distinguishes plasticity from flexibility. A flexible material takes any form imposed on it and silently holds it. A plastic one is capable of resisting: an imprint may remain, but the form doesn’t have to match the mold that was forced on it. In other words, humiliation is an attempt to turn you into a flexible material that must accept a “lower” form. The pain of humiliation is a sign that your form did not consent. That refusal to consent is your dignity, even if outwardly you said nothing at the time.
humiliation.practice: Stand up and slowly straighten to your full height, opening your shoulders — feel your real form. Tell yourself: “They tried to make me smaller, but I am who I am.”

body_shame.text: An old oak table keeps its scratches, stains and dents — and is loved more than a new one precisely for them. Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background, and behind it lies real pressure: advertising, comparisons, other people’s remarks. The culture of flexibility that Malabou describes turns the body, too, into a project that must be endlessly adjusted to a template. But for Malabou, form is not a predetermined ideal but a history: it takes shape from what we have lived through, from chance, from what has happened to us. Your body carries the traces of your life — births, work, illnesses, joys, years. These are not deviations from a norm but your very form, one of a kind. You may not love every feature and still stop seeing your body as defective, and see it instead as a chronicle.
body_shame.practice: Choose one feature of your body and tell yourself its story, like a chronicler — without judgment.

illness.text: A tree grows crooked after a storm, but it grows, and the forest accepts it as it is. Illness, when your body lets you down, is a hard experience: it is frightening, painful, it seems your former self has vanished — and all these feelings are legitimate. In Ontology of the Accident, Malabou writes about events that change a person without their choosing, and calls this destructive plasticity. Her important thought: the new form that arises after such an event is not simply a “spoiled copy” of the old one but another way of being, which deserves attention and respect. Then illness is neither a betrayal by your body nor your fault, but an accident you now live with. You can grieve the possibilities you once had and at the same time come to know your present self — no less real than before.
illness.practice: Rest your palm on the part of your body that is struggling right now and tell it: “I’m getting to know you again.”

pride.text: A potter stamps a mark on the bottom of a jug — not from vanity, but because their trace is there. Pride in what you have done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there is no need to hide it. Plasticity, for Malabou, has a second meaning — the capacity to give form, as a sculptor gives form to material. Pride is the moment you see your own form in what you have created. Malabou draws on Hegel, for whom spirit recognizes itself in its works: a person doesn’t just think about themselves but finds themselves in what they have done, out in the world. Through this lens, healthy pride is a recognition: “my trace is here.” It has no need to belittle others. You can let yourself fully enjoy what you have done — this too is part of how a form grows stronger.
pride.practice: Put your “mark” on what you have made: say aloud where your own trace is in it — a decision, an effort, a style.

quote.text: Nothing great in the world has been accomplished without passion.
quote.author: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
quote.source: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction

melancholy.text: Evening light makes the outlines of things especially sharp — as if a form were saying goodbye by showing itself whole. A bright sadness, melancholy, is a quiet, slightly sad and yet warm state, and it doesn’t need fixing. One of Malabou’s books is called Plasticity at the Dusk of Writing: in it she writes about the passage from one era of thought to another, when the old still glows and the new is only beginning to show through. It follows that melancholy is the feeling of such a dusk: some form of your life is leaving, and the next has not yet taken shape. There is no catastrophe in this sadness — only a sense of transition. Malabou sees form not as a frozen object but as a living process in which farewell and birth go side by side. You can live through melancholy as twilight: unhurriedly, letting each shade be noticed.
melancholy.practice: In the evening, go to a window or outside and watch the light change. Silently name one form of your life that is quietly leaving now.
